questions.stem: A stakeholder says, "Make the support assistant much smarter." What is the best next step?

options.text: Choose the highest-capability model and compare several prompt variants.
options.explanation: That is a design choice made before the team has defined what success means.

options.text: Enable streaming so users see the first tokens of an answer sooner.
options.explanation: Streaming may help a latency target, but no target has been stated yet.

options.text: Define measurable functional and non-functional success criteria.
options.explanation: The team needs testable behavior plus targets such as quality, safety, latency, and cost before selecting an architecture.

options.text: Build a vector database that covers every support article.
options.explanation: Retrieval may be useful, but it is not a substitute for defining the problem and acceptance criteria.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A team must reduce support handling time while keeping responses safe and affordable. Which statements are valid requirements rather than design decisions? Select THREE.

options.text: At least 90% of evaluated answers meet the support-quality rubric.
options.explanation: This is a measurable quality target that can be evaluated against a defined test set.

options.text: Use streaming responses with a fast model.
options.explanation: This is an implementation approach that might satisfy latency requirements, not a requirement itself.

options.text: The p95 time to first visible response is under two seconds.
options.explanation: A percentile, a metric, and a threshold make this a testable non-functional requirement that any architecture can be checked against.

options.text: The assistant should feel helpful to most customers.
options.explanation: This is an aspiration until it is tied to a rubric, rate, population, and threshold.

options.text: Monthly model spend must stay below the approved budget ceiling.
options.explanation: This is a measurable cost constraint that architecture choices must respect.

questions.rationale: Tests functional and non-functional requirements versus solution choices.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A production team plans to replace a deprecated model before its retirement date. Which sequence is strongest?

options.text: Export usage to find callers, test the replacement against evals, then roll out and monitor.
options.explanation: This identifies the blast radius, validates behavior before migration, and closes the loop with operational observation.

options.text: Change the model ID in production first, then investigate regressions only if users report them.
options.explanation: A model migration can change output and parameter compatibility, so production should not be the first test environment.

options.text: Wait until requests start failing at retirement, then switch every caller to the newest model.
options.explanation: Retirement is a scheduled dependency event, not an incident that should be discovered by failure.

options.text: Keep the old model in place because deprecated models remain supported after retirement.
options.explanation: Deprecated models still work temporarily but have a retirement date and must be migrated.

questions.rationale: Tests eval-driven lifecycle management for model changes.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A batch client receives HTTP 429 with no Retry-After header and error.details.error_code set to enforced_spend_limit_reached. What should it do?

options.text: Stop retrying and surface the spend-cap condition for a limit or tier change.
options.explanation: A spend-cap 429 has no Retry-After and does not self-resolve on an ordinary backoff schedule.

options.text: Retry rapidly because 429 always represents a short rate-limit window.
options.explanation: This 429 denotes a tier spend cap, so rapid retries only consume attempts without restoring access.

options.text: Shrink the request payload until it no longer exceeds the model's context window.
options.explanation: An oversized request is a 400 or 413 class issue, not this spend-cap signal.

options.text: Re-authenticate with a freshly issued API key and resend the same request.
options.explanation: Authentication failures are 401 errors; the response identifies an account spending condition.

questions.rationale: Tests the distinction between retryable rate limits and spend-cap responses.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: An app receives HTTP 200 from the Messages API. Which response conditions still require application-specific handling rather than treating the call as a completed answer? Select THREE.

options.text: The response includes a request-id header.
options.explanation: Request IDs support observability and support cases; they do not signal an incomplete answer.

options.text: stop_reason is refusal.
options.explanation: A refusal is a successful transport response but not a usable task completion, so it needs a product fallback or message.

options.text: usage.output_tokens is nonzero.
options.explanation: Nonzero output usage is normal and does not by itself require a recovery path.

options.text: stop_reason is max_tokens.
options.explanation: This indicates output truncation at the configured cap and may require continuation or a larger cap.

options.text: stop_reason is tool_use.
options.explanation: The client must execute the requested tool and send a tool_result to continue the loop.

questions.rationale: Tests transport success versus response semantics.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A streamed request starts successfully, then emits an SSE error event with overloaded_error. Which handling is correct?

options.text: Ignore it because the initial HTTP status was 200 and the stream already began delivering text.
options.explanation: Streaming can fail after headers are sent, so status-code handling alone is insufficient.

options.text: Treat it as a malformed tool result and resend the previous tool output as a new turn.
options.explanation: A tool-result continuation is for a tool_use response, not an overloaded stream.

options.text: Convert it to a successful empty answer because text may have already arrived.
options.explanation: Partial text is not proof that the requested operation completed correctly.

options.text: Treat it as the streamed equivalent of a retryable 529 and apply bounded backoff.
options.explanation: overloaded_error is a transient capacity condition; stream consumers must handle it as an in-band error.

questions.rationale: Tests SSE error handling after HTTP success.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A client uses prompt caching. usage reports input_tokens: 80, cache_creation_input_tokens: 0, and cache_read_input_tokens: 120000. Which statement is accurate?

options.text: Total input is 120080 tokens; the cached read is billed at a reduced rate and usually excluded from ITPM.
options.explanation: Total input includes uncached, cache-write, and cache-read tokens; cache reads typically do not count toward ITPM.

options.text: The prompt was only 80 tokens in total, so this request comfortably fits inside any model's context window.
options.explanation: input_tokens excludes the cached prefix, which still occupies context-window capacity.

options.text: The 120000 cached tokens are neither billed nor counted against ITPM, and no longer occupy context.
options.explanation: Caching reduces price and rate-limit impact; it does not make tokens free or remove them from context.

options.text: The cache was missed on this request, because a cache_creation_input_tokens value of zero means no entry exists.
options.explanation: A positive cache_read_input_tokens value is direct evidence of a cache hit.

questions.rationale: Tests interpretation of cache-aware usage fields.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: An agent calls create_refund after Claude requests it. The network drops just after the provider may have accepted the refund. What prevents a duplicate refund on retry?

options.text: Use an idempotency key or deduplicate the tool execution by its stable operation ID.
options.explanation: The tool handler must make repeated delivery of the same logical operation safe.

options.text: Retry the Messages API call with a larger max_tokens so the tool call completes.
options.explanation: The duplicate comes from re-executing an external side effect, so a bigger output budget on the model call changes nothing about the refund being sent twice.

options.text: Set temperature to zero before calling the refund tool so the model requests it once.
options.explanation: Sampling settings do not provide exactly-once behavior for an external payment action.

options.text: Persist the refund outcome only in the model conversation history and re-read it on retry.
options.explanation: Transactional state needs an authoritative system of record, not transient context.

questions.rationale: Tests idempotency at the side-effect boundary.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A developer wraps an SDK call in a three-attempt retry helper without changing SDK settings. The SDK already retries transient failures twice. What is the main problem?

options.text: The SDK will detect the outer loop and disable its own retries, leaving three attempts.
options.explanation: The SDK cannot infer the external wrapper and continues its configured retry policy.

options.text: The request becomes effectively deterministic because the same call is repeated.
options.explanation: Repeating a request changes neither sampling behavior nor correctness guarantees.

options.text: The request can make up to nine attempts, amplifying load and rate-limit pressure.
options.explanation: Each outer attempt can invoke the SDK's initial call plus two retries, multiplying traffic for one logical operation.

options.text: Only authentication errors will be retried nine times; transient errors stop after two.
options.explanation: Authentication errors are terminal; the multiplication concerns transient errors the SDK retries.

questions.rationale: Tests avoidance of stacked retry policies.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A service launches 2,000 independent model calls at once and receives many 429s. Which changes are appropriate? Select THREE.

options.text: Use asyncio.gather without limits because asynchronous code should maximize parallelism.
options.explanation: Async concurrency still consumes RPM, ITPM, and OTPM; unbounded fan-out is the failure mode.

options.text: Retry 400 invalid_request_error responses with the same payload.
options.explanation: A malformed request is deterministic and must be fixed rather than retried.

options.text: Use a bounded worker pool or semaphore sized to observed rate limits.
options.explanation: Bounded concurrency applies backpressure instead of producing an uncontrolled burst.

options.text: Add exponential backoff with jitter for genuinely retryable failures.
options.explanation: Jitter reduces synchronized retry storms while backoff gives capacity time to recover.

options.text: Log rate-limit headers to tune the pool and monitor headroom.
options.explanation: The response headers expose the capacity signals needed to choose safe concurrency.

questions.rationale: Tests bounded concurrency and retry discipline.

questions.stem: A regression test compares two JSON model responses as raw strings and fails only because object-key order changed. What should the test do?

options.text: Parse the JSON and compare the required object structure and values.
options.explanation: JSON object key order and whitespace are serialization details; structural comparison tests the contract.

options.text: Raise temperature so the model emits keys in a consistent order.
options.explanation: Sampling does not turn a serialized JSON string into a stable contractual representation.

options.text: Store the original string in conversation history for the next test run.
options.explanation: History is not a test oracle and cannot solve serialization variation.

options.text: Disable all SDK retries so the response string cannot change between runs.
options.explanation: Retries are unrelated to JSON object ordering in successful responses.

questions.rationale: Tests robust validation of structured outputs.

questions.stem: An application must generate a draft, run deterministic business-rule checks, and send only passing drafts to a reviewer. Which design best satisfies that requirement?

options.text: An autonomous agent that reads each draft and decides whether the business rules need checking.
options.explanation: The business-rule gate is mandatory and known in advance, so leaving it to agent discretion weakens the requirement.

options.text: A code-defined workflow that invokes the model and runs the business-rule checks as explicit gates.
options.explanation: Known validation stages belong in application control flow, where each gate can be tested and audited.

options.text: A Message Batch that generates all drafts asynchronously, since several drafts may be produced per run.
options.explanation: Batching changes delivery timing and price; it does not provide deterministic validation gates.

options.text: Prompt caching of the business rules, so the model applies the same rule set consistently to every draft.
options.explanation: Caching may optimize repeated context but cannot execute or enforce application business rules.

questions.rationale: Tests deterministic application validation gates around model output.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A legal-answer feature must return source citations from PDFs and also emit a strict JSON response schema in one call. What should the team expect?

options.text: Both can be enabled together in one request, because citations are emitted as ordinary text fields inside the JSON.
options.explanation: Citations and JSON outputs are incompatible in the same Messages API request.

options.text: Prefill an assistant message with an opening brace while citations are enabled, so the model emits JSON around them.
options.explanation: Prefill is not the current structured-output mechanism and is rejected on newer models.

options.text: Use a larger context window model, because the conflict is caused by the size of the PDFs, not the features.
options.explanation: The limitation is an API feature incompatibility, not a context-capacity issue.

options.text: Use two stages or redesign the response, because citations and JSON outputs cannot be combined in one request.
options.explanation: The system must separate sourcing from strict schema formatting when both guarantees are required.

questions.rationale: Tests output contracts and feature compatibility.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A product team is selecting techniques for a large, frequently changing knowledge base. Which statements are correct? Select THREE.

options.text: RAG retrieves a relevant subset and can provide current facts at request time.
options.explanation: Retrieval is appropriate when knowledge changes or the corpus is too large to include wholesale.

options.text: Prompt caching reduces the cost of a repeated prefix but does not reduce its context-window footprint.
options.explanation: Caching changes billing and ITPM accounting, while the cached material still occupies the model context.

options.text: A one-million-token window makes retrieval unnecessary for accuracy.
options.explanation: Large contexts can suffer context rot, and selective retrieval remains useful for relevance and freshness.

options.text: The Messages API remembers prior sessions automatically once a document is sent once.
options.explanation: The API is stateless; the application owns history and must send relevant context each request.

options.text: A shared static policy can be a candidate for prompt caching.
options.explanation: A stable repeated prefix is exactly the scenario prompt caching is designed to optimize.

questions.rationale: Tests RAG, statelessness, context, and caching trade-offs.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A job must summarize 60,000 records overnight, users do not wait for results, and cost matters. Which API mode best fits?

options.text: Synchronous streaming Messages requests per record.
options.explanation: Streaming improves interactive perceived latency, which this offline workload does not require.

options.text: The Message Batches API, with one request per record.
options.explanation: The Batches API is built for asynchronous bulk work: results arrive within a processing window rather than immediately, and token usage is billed at a discounted batch rate.

options.text: A single long conversation containing all of the records.
options.explanation: A giant conversation is not a reliable bulk-processing strategy and can exceed practical context limits.

options.text: An interactive Claude Code session pointed at the data.
options.explanation: Claude Code is an agentic developer product, not the delivery mechanism for a production record batch.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A production configuration references a model by a short alias that the provider may point at a newer snapshot over time. The team wants reproducible behavior across releases. What is the best change?

options.text: Keep the alias and add more few-shot examples to the prompt so behavior stays stable.
options.explanation: Examples may improve behavior but do not prevent the alias from resolving to a new model version.

options.text: Replace the model ID with the organization API key, which is bound to a model.
options.explanation: Credentials authenticate a request; they do not determine model-version reproducibility.

options.text: Pin the evaluated dated snapshot model ID in configuration and version control.
options.explanation: A dated snapshot identifies the exact evaluated model, while a short alias can advance to a newer snapshot.

options.text: Switch to a different undated alias that the provider updates on a slower cadence.
options.explanation: Any undated alias can be re-pointed by the provider, so swapping one alias for another does not pin the evaluated model.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A repository needs shared coding guidance that the team can review and version, while each developer keeps personal local preferences. What is the best arrangement?

options.text: Put every preference, shared and personal, only in one senior developer's local settings file for others to copy.
options.explanation: Local-only settings cannot provide a shared, versioned team convention.

options.text: Embed the shared guidance in every prompt sent during a session, and let each developer add personal notes to the same prompt.
options.explanation: Repeated prompt text is harder to review and maintain than scoped project configuration.

options.text: Encode all coding conventions as deny hooks in the repository, and keep personal preferences as additional hooks in user settings.
options.explanation: Hooks are appropriate for deterministic execution controls, not ordinary explanatory team guidance.

options.text: Store shared repository guidance in versioned project instructions or settings, and keep personal preferences in local user settings.
options.explanation: This gives the team a reviewable shared baseline without forcing personal preferences into repository configuration.

questions.rationale: Tests versioned project guidance versus personal local configuration and enforcement hooks.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: Which content contributes to a Messages API request's context-window budget?

options.text: Only the user's message text and the final assistant answer; tools and history are separate.
options.explanation: This omits system instructions, tools, history, multimodal inputs, and reasoning output.

options.text: Only uncached input tokens; anything served from the prompt cache is outside the budget.
options.explanation: Cached tokens are still present in context; caching does not create additional window capacity.

options.text: System prompt, history, tool schemas and results, multimodal inputs, and generated output.
options.explanation: All of these consume the finite context budget, including cached content and thinking output.

options.text: Only the tokens counted by usage.input_tokens, since that field is the request's context size.
options.explanation: That field excludes cache reads and writes, so it is not the full context size.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A model’s API documentation says it uses adaptive thinking and rejects legacy manual thinking budgets. A request sends thinking.type set to enabled with budget_tokens and receives a 400. What should the client do?

options.text: Increase the fixed budget_tokens value step by step until the request is accepted.
options.explanation: The request uses an unsupported configuration form, so a larger value cannot make it valid.

options.text: Set temperature to zero before retrying with the legacy thinking configuration.
options.explanation: Sampling controls do not change which thinking configuration the documented model interface accepts.

options.text: Add an assistant prefill before enabling the legacy thinking configuration.
options.explanation: Prefill is unrelated to the request-schema incompatibility and does not convert legacy manual thinking into adaptive thinking.

options.text: Use the model’s adaptive-thinking configuration and its documented effort control.
options.explanation: The documented capability contract, rather than a model-generation label, determines the valid request shape.

questions.rationale: Tests adaptive versus legacy extended thinking.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A team sets temperature to 0 and uses exact-string assertions for generated summaries. Tests are flaky. What is the best correction?

options.text: Test required structure, factual criteria, and rubric outcomes across representative cases.
options.explanation: Non-deterministic language output should be evaluated by properties and distributions, not byte-for-byte prose.

options.text: Assume a platform defect because temperature zero guarantees identical output for identical input.
options.explanation: The documentation explicitly states that identical inputs can still produce different outputs at temperature zero.

options.text: Raise max_tokens until every summary is identical, since truncation is what varies between runs.
options.explanation: A larger output cap prevents truncation but cannot make sampling deterministic.

options.text: Store the first successful output as a permanent golden string and assert equality.
options.explanation: A single sampled wording is a brittle oracle for an open-ended summarization task.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A chatbot answers questions about policies changed yesterday. Its prompt is well-written but answers are stale. What best addresses the root problem?

options.text: Lower temperature to eliminate hallucinated policy details in the answers.
options.explanation: Sampling does not supply missing facts and cannot eliminate hallucination.

options.text: Use retrieval to supply current policy material at request time.
options.explanation: The problem is missing current knowledge; retrieval grounds the answer in an external up-to-date source.

options.text: Fine-tune the model through the Claude API after every policy edit.
options.explanation: Retraining is the wrong tool for facts that change daily: it is slow and expensive where available, and Claude's first-party API is used through prompting and retrieval rather than a fine-tuning endpoint.

options.text: Increase max_tokens so the model can recall more training data.
options.explanation: max_tokens controls generated output, not the knowledge available to the model.

questions.rationale: Tests prompting, retrieval, and model knowledge distinctions.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: Users say a long answer feels slow because no visible user-facing text appears for several seconds, though total generation time is acceptable. Which measure and change are most relevant?

options.text: Measure time to first visible text and stream user-facing response text.
options.explanation: Time to first visible text measures the stated experience; streaming can expose user-facing text before the full response completes.

options.text: Measure only total generated tokens and disable streaming to reduce overhead.
options.explanation: Total tokens do not isolate the delay before users see text, and disabling streaming worsens that experience.

options.text: Measure per-request cost and move the request to the Batches API.
options.explanation: Batch requests are asynchronous and cannot improve an interactive first-visible-text delay.

options.text: Measure cache hit rate and cache the answer in the model's permanent memory.
options.explanation: The API has no permanent answer memory, and caching does not itself guarantee early visible output.

questions.rationale: Tests TTFT versus total latency and streaming.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A retrieval system has weak ranking quality. Which changes are sound? Select THREE.

options.text: Embed source documents as documents and user searches as queries when the embedding provider distinguishes them.
options.explanation: Document and query embeddings can be optimized for their different roles; mixing the modes can degrade retrieval.

options.text: Use a reranker to reorder retrieved candidates by relevance.
options.explanation: Reranking is a separate relevance-improvement stage after initial candidate retrieval.

options.text: Ask the generative Messages API to return embeddings for the vector store.
options.explanation: Claude's Messages API is generative; Anthropic does not provide its own embedding model through it.

options.text: Put the entire corpus in every prompt because a larger context always improves recall.
options.explanation: Large contexts cost more and can suffer context rot, so relevance selection remains important.

options.text: Attach citations or quotes to grounded answers when users need to verify source support.
options.explanation: Grounding with verifiable source evidence helps users distinguish supported claims from unsupported output.

questions.rationale: Tests RAG pipeline components and grounding.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A high-volume real-time classifier has simple inputs, a tight latency budget, and evals show the fastest tier meets the quality threshold. Which selection principle applies?

options.text: Always choose the most capable model because it has the largest context window.
options.explanation: A larger or more capable tier is not justified when the workload and evals do not require it.

options.text: Choose a batch-only configuration because the request volume is high.
options.explanation: High volume does not remove the real-time latency requirement, which rules out asynchronous batch delivery.

options.text: Use a floating alias so the classifier receives silent capability upgrades.
options.explanation: Production behavior should be pinned to the evaluated model identifier rather than a drifting alias.

options.text: Use the lower-cost, faster model that passes the task-specific evals.
options.explanation: Model choice should follow requirements and measured capability; over-provisioning wastes cost and latency.

questions.rationale: Tests requirement- and eval-based model selection.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A nightly job processes many independent records with a large shared rubric. Which choices reduce cost without sacrificing the offline requirement? Select THREE.

options.text: Use the Message Batches API for the asynchronous work.
options.explanation: Batch processing is designed for offline workloads and bills token usage at a discounted batch rate compared with synchronous requests.

options.text: Place an explicit cache breakpoint after the shared static rubric.
options.explanation: A stable shared prefix is the part that can be reused across requests for reduced input cost.

options.text: Use the one-hour cache TTL when processing may span longer than five minutes.
options.explanation: The longer TTL is appropriate for shared context reused with gaps beyond the default five-minute lifetime.

options.text: Enable stream: true inside each batch request.
options.explanation: Streaming is unsupported in Message Batches and is unnecessary for an offline job.

options.text: Assume batch results preserve submission order and zip them to inputs.
options.explanation: Batch results can arrive in any order and must be matched with their custom_id.

questions.rationale: Tests batch, caching layout, and batch-result handling.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A team adds cache_control to an 800-token shared prompt on a model whose minimum cacheable length is 1024 tokens. Both cache usage fields remain zero. What happened?

options.text: The request failed validation because cache_control requires a prefix of at least 1024 tokens.
options.explanation: Being below the threshold is a silent cache miss, not an invalid request.

options.text: The API silently processed the prompt without caching because it was below the minimum.
options.explanation: Short prefixes do not produce an error; the usage fields reveal that no cache write or read occurred.

options.text: The response exceeded max_tokens, so the cache entry was evicted before usage came back.
options.explanation: Output truncation and the cacheable-prefix threshold are separate mechanisms.

options.text: The prompt was cached, but cache reads are reported in headers rather than in usage.
options.explanation: Cache creation and read token fields are the documented way to verify caching behavior.

questions.rationale: Tests minimum cacheable lengths and observability.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A developer is in the middle of a long refactor and needs to retain the task context while freeing window space. Which Claude Code command is appropriate?

options.text: /clear, because it keeps the active conversation intact.
options.explanation: Clear starts a new empty conversation; the old session is resumable but not active context.

options.text: /rewind, because it summarizes the oldest messages.
options.explanation: Rewind restores checkpoints; it is not a context-management summarization command.

options.text: /compact with focused instructions about the refactor.
options.explanation: Compaction summarizes the current conversation so the same task can continue with less context.

options.text: /usage, because it trims token use automatically.
options.explanation: Usage reports consumption but does not change the context in the current session.

questions.stem: A repository must block a dangerous shell pattern every time Claude Code attempts it. Why is a blocking PreToolUse hook preferable to a sentence in CLAUDE.md?

options.text: Hooks are deterministic lifecycle automation and can deny the matching tool call.
options.explanation: A PreToolUse hook runs at the execution event and can enforce a block instead of relying on model interpretation.

options.text: CLAUDE.md is ignored whenever a hooks configuration exists in the project.
options.explanation: CLAUDE.md still provides useful project context; it simply is not an enforcement mechanism.

options.text: Hooks make the model's output deterministic, so it can no longer propose the pattern.
options.explanation: Hooks control lifecycle behavior, not the stochastic generation process.

options.text: A hook is a documentation format for reusable prompts that the model reads more reliably.
options.explanation: Reusable prompt procedures are skills; hooks execute configured actions on lifecycle events.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A team wants Claude to fix failing tests in a repository. The number of edit-and-rerun cycles cannot be predicted, and each cycle's test output shows whether progress was made. Which approach fits best?

options.text: A fixed prompt chain that analyses the failures, applies one edit, runs the tests once, and reports the outcome.
options.explanation: A fixed chain assumes the path is known in advance; a single edit-and-run pass cannot adapt when the first attempt does not make the tests pass.

options.text: An autonomous agent loop that edits, runs the tests, reads the results, and stops on a pass or an iteration cap.
options.explanation: Unpredictable step counts with verifiable environment feedback are the documented case for an agent loop, with a stopping condition to keep it bounded.

options.text: A single Messages API call with the whole repository attached, asked to output the fully corrected source tree.
options.explanation: One call gives the model no test feedback, so it cannot verify or correct its own edits and errors compound silently.

options.text: A routing step that classifies each failure by category and applies a pre-written canned fix for that category.
options.explanation: Routing dispatches to specialised handlers but still cannot iterate against test results; canned fixes do not adapt to what the suite reports.

questions.rationale: Tests recognising when an agent (not a workflow) is the right architecture: open-ended steps plus ground-truth feedback.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A lead agent delegates market, policy, and technical research to three workers. The final recommendation must be traceable and have one accountable decision-maker. Which architecture best fits?

options.text: Let every worker independently edit the shared final recommendation as its research completes.
options.explanation: Independent edits create conflicting authority and obscure how evidence conflicts were resolved.

options.text: Give all workers the full lead transcript and let responsibilities emerge from the conversation.
options.explanation: Shared context does not establish ownership, scopes, or an escalation path.

options.text: A supervisor agent assigns bounded tasks, collects evidence, and owns synthesis and escalation.
options.explanation: A supervisor preserves one accountable owner for synthesis while delegating bounded evidence gathering.

options.text: Have every worker run the same broad research task and vote on which final answer to return.
options.explanation: Duplicated broad work wastes capacity and leaves no deliberate division of expertise.

questions.rationale: Tests supervisor ownership, bounded delegation, and accountable synthesis in a multi-agent architecture.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: What belongs in every prompt to a context-isolated research subagent? Select TWO.

options.text: A concrete objective and scope boundary
options.explanation: A subagent starts with a fresh context, so without an explicit objective and scope it will duplicate sibling work or wander into irrelevant research.

options.text: A required output format and source guidance
options.explanation: The lead has to merge many workers' output, so telling each worker the deliverable shape and what sources count keeps results comparable and citable.

options.text: The entire parent transcript
options.explanation: The point of context isolation is that the worker does not carry the parent's full history; pasting the transcript spends the worker's window on material it does not need.

options.text: Every intermediate tool result verbatim
options.explanation: Bulky intermediate results belong in a store or summary that the worker can fetch if needed; forwarding them verbatim crowds out the actual task.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: Two client tool calls arrive in one response; one succeeds and one fails validation. What must the next request contain?

options.text: One tool result for the success now, and the failed call's result after the model replies
options.explanation: Splitting the results across two turns leaves one tool_use block without a matching tool_result in that turn, which the API rejects as malformed.

options.text: Only the successful result, since the failed call produced nothing usable
options.explanation: Omitting the failed call's result leaves a tool_use block unanswered, violating the requirement that every tool call in a turn receives a corresponding result.

options.text: Two assistant-role messages, each carrying one tool result and its tool_use_id
options.explanation: Tool results must be returned as user-role content blocks, not assistant-role messages, which represent the model's own output.

options.text: One user message with both matching tool results and is_error for the failure
options.explanation: Every tool_use block must get a matching tool_result in the same next turn, and the failed call must be marked is_error so the model treats it as a failure rather than a normal result.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A Claude Agent SDK run is configured with max_turns set to 8. The final ResultMessage has subtype error_max_turns. How should the harness interpret this?

options.text: The model produced a complete final answer, but the SDK truncated the returned transcript to the last eight messages before handing it back.
options.explanation: max_turns limits how many tool-use turns run, not the length of a text answer; an error subtype means no successful result was produced.

options.text: The Messages API rejected the request because max_turns is not a valid parameter, so the harness should remove it and resend the same prompt.
options.explanation: max_turns is an SDK-level loop control and never reaches the Messages API, so the API cannot reject it; the run completed but hit the cap.

options.text: The agent exhausted its tool-use turn budget before finishing; no result text is present and the harness must decide whether to resume or fail.
options.explanation: max_turns counts tool-use turns, and hitting it produces an error subtype whose result text is absent, so the harness owns the recovery decision rather than treating the output as an answer.

options.text: The eighth tool call failed with an error, so the harness should retry that single tool call and then continue the loop from the same point.
options.explanation: The subtype reports budget exhaustion, not a tool failure; a single tool error would surface as a tool_result marked is_error inside the loop.

questions.rationale: Tests understanding of SDK termination guarantees (max_turns) and how result subtypes are read.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to documented blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A response stops at max_tokens while emitting an incomplete tool call. What recovery is correct?

options.text: Execute the partial JSON, filling gaps with null
options.explanation: Partial JSON is not a valid tool call payload, and filling gaps with null risks executing the tool with unintended or unsafe arguments.

options.text: Retry with higher max_tokens so the call is regenerated
options.explanation: A response cut off at max_tokens contains a syntactically incomplete tool call, so the reliable fix is regenerating the whole response with enough budget to complete it.

options.text: Return a successful tool result so the model can continue
options.explanation: There is no complete tool_use to respond to since the call never finished emitting, so fabricating a success result would desynchronize the conversation from what the model actually requested.

options.text: Treat it as pause_turn and resend the conversation as is
options.explanation: pause_turn describes a server-tool long-running pause, not a client response truncated by hitting the token limit; the two stop reasons require different handling.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A support system classifies requests then sends each category to specialized prompts and tools. What pattern is this?

options.text: Prompt chaining
options.explanation: Prompt chaining runs a fixed sequence of steps on every input; it does not branch to different specialized handling based on category.

options.text: Parallel voting
options.explanation: Voting runs multiple attempts at the same task and aggregates results; it does not classify then dispatch to different specialists.

options.text: Routing workflow
options.explanation: Classifying an input and directing it to a specialized prompt or tool per category is the defining behavior of the routing pattern.

options.text: Evaluator optimizer
options.explanation: This pattern iterates one output against a critique loop; it does not describe classification-driven dispatch to different prompts.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A translation draft is critiqued by a separate model and revised until a clear rubric passes. What pattern fits?

options.text: An evaluator-optimizer loop
options.explanation: A separate model critiquing the draft against a rubric and driving revisions until it passes is the defining evaluator-optimizer cycle.

options.text: A parallel sectioning workflow
options.explanation: Sectioning splits one task into independent parallel subtasks; it does not describe an iterative critique-and-revise cycle against a rubric.

options.text: Static model selection up front
options.explanation: Choosing a fixed model up front says nothing about an iterative critique-revise loop driving the draft toward passing a rubric.

options.text: A single programmatic gate
options.explanation: A single pass/fail code check has no revision step; the scenario requires a separate critiquing model driving iterative rewrites, not a one-shot gate.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: An agent loads complete records from 40 tools and increasingly misses key facts. What change best fixes the cause?

options.text: Raise max_tokens so the model has room to reason over every loaded record
options.explanation: max_tokens caps the length of the model's output, not the volume of loaded tool data, so it does not address records crowding out key facts.

options.text: Return compact high-signal fields and retrieve detail just in time
options.explanation: Loading full records from every tool floods context with low-signal detail, so returning compact fields and fetching specifics only when needed keeps attention on what matters.

options.text: Move all the complete records into the system prompt for stable placement
options.explanation: Moving the same bulk of unfiltered records into the system prompt still floods context with irrelevant detail; it does not reduce what is loaded.

options.text: Add an instruction telling the model to track key facts carefully
options.explanation: An instruction cannot compensate for context genuinely overloaded with low-signal data; the fix is reducing what is loaded, not asking the model to try harder.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A long conversation needs a condensed narrative state instead of deletion of old tool results. Which mechanism fits?

options.text: Clearing older tool results
options.explanation: Clearing tool results discards content instead of condensing it into a narrative state, which is the opposite of what the scenario asks for.

options.text: Additional few-shot input examples
options.explanation: Adding examples increases prompt content rather than reducing an already-long conversation, so it does not solve a context-length problem.

options.text: An assistant-turn prefill message
options.explanation: Prefill constrains how the assistant's next reply begins; it has no effect on how much prior conversation history is retained.

options.text: Server-side context compaction
options.explanation: Compaction produces a condensed summary of the conversation so far while preserving its narrative continuity, which is exactly the requirement instead of deleting old data outright.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: Where should standing role instructions go in a Messages API request?

options.text: A message with the system role
options.explanation: The Messages API messages array only accepts user and assistant roles; there is no system-role message to place instructions in.

options.text: The top-level system parameter
options.explanation: The Messages API accepts a dedicated top-level system field precisely for standing role and behavior instructions, kept separate from the turn-by-turn messages array.

options.text: A tool_result content block
options.explanation: Tool result blocks carry the output of a specific tool call, not standing behavioral instructions for the whole conversation.

options.text: The stop_sequences parameter
options.explanation: A stop sequence only tells the API when to stop generating text; it carries no instructional content at all.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A current model rejects an assistant-turn JSON prefill. What should enforce a fixed JSON reply shape?

options.text: temperature zero plus the same prefill
options.explanation: Lowering temperature only makes sampling more deterministic; it does not restore acceptance of a prefill technique the current model rejects.

options.text: An opening brace inside a tool_result block
options.explanation: A tool result is data returned from a tool call, not a mechanism for constraining the shape of the model's own reply.

options.text: output_config.format with a JSON Schema
options.explanation: A structured-output configuration constrains generation against a declared schema at the API level, which is the supported replacement once the model no longer accepts assistant-turn prefill.

options.text: A longer stop sequence after the closing brace
options.explanation: A stop sequence only truncates output at a matched string; it cannot enforce that the output conforms to a JSON structure.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: For a 90k-token contract and five questions, what structure follows long-context guidance?

options.text: Documents first, query last, with a quotes-first grounding step
options.explanation: Placing long reference material before the question and asking for grounding quotes first improves retrieval accuracy over that material, consistent with long-context best practice.

options.text: Questions first, then the documents, with a direct-answer instruction
options.explanation: Putting the questions before a 90k-token document works against the model's attention pattern for long-context retrieval, which favors documents preceding the query.

options.text: An exhaustive system-prompt summary of the contract instead of its text
options.explanation: A summary in the system prompt discards the contract's actual text the five questions need to be answered against, trading recall for compression.

options.text: Temperature zero for retrieval, with the documents in any order
options.explanation: Temperature only affects sampling randomness in generation; it has no role in how content is retrieved from a long context window.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A structured-output extraction returns HTTP 200 with stop_reason refusal. What must the client assume?

options.text: The schema is guaranteed to be satisfied, because HTTP 200 means success
options.explanation: A 200 status confirms the API call succeeded at the transport level, not that the model produced schema-conformant content; a refusal can still occur with that status.

options.text: The content may be unusable; inspect stop_reason and handle refusal
options.explanation: HTTP 200 only means the request was received; stop_reason communicates whether the model actually completed the requested output, so refusal must be checked and handled separately from transport status.

options.text: Identical retries with the same payload will repair it on a later attempt
options.explanation: A refusal reflects the model declining the request as posed, so resending the identical request is likely to produce the same refusal rather than fix it.

options.text: It is a transient rate limit reported in-band, so back off and retry
options.explanation: Rate limiting is signaled through HTTP 429 responses, not a 200 response carrying a refusal stop_reason, so this misattributes the cause.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: Claude picks a client tool in the wrong situations despite a good schema. What improves selection most?

options.text: A detailed description explaining use, non-use, parameters, and limits
options.explanation: The model selects tools primarily from the natural-language description, so clarifying when to use it, when not to, and its parameter limits directly improves selection accuracy.

options.text: Setting strict to true on the input schema and dropping the description
options.explanation: Strict schema enforcement only validates the shape of arguments once a tool is chosen; it gives the model no guidance on when that tool is the right one to pick.

options.text: A top-level switch that disables parallel tool use so calls run one at a time
options.explanation: Controlling whether tools can be called in parallel affects execution concurrency, not which tool the model judges appropriate for a given situation.

options.text: Returning every database field from the tool so the model sees more context
options.explanation: The volume of data a tool returns after being called has no bearing on the model's decision of whether to call that tool in the first place.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A create_transfer client tool can move money. Its input carries an action field plus account and amount details. Which implementation controls are required to reject malformed or unauthorized calls before a transfer is made? Select THREE.

options.text: Restrict the action field to an enum of supported operations.
options.explanation: An enum rejects action names outside the handler contract before execution.

options.text: Require the source account, destination account, and amount in the tool input schema.
options.explanation: Required fields prevent an incomplete transfer request from reaching execution.

options.text: Validate account existence, authorization, and business limits in the server-side handler.
options.explanation: JSON Schema cannot establish identity, permissions, balances, or policy limits; the trusted handler must enforce them.

options.text: Rely on a detailed tool description as the only validation mechanism.
options.explanation: A description guides model selection but cannot reject malformed arguments or authorize a money movement.

questions.rationale: Tests the boundary between JSON Schema argument validation and server-side semantic and authorization checks.
questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: Why can forced named tool choice fail with manual extended thinking?

options.text: Tool choice must never be set when thinking is enabled; even auto and none are rejected
options.explanation: Tool choice can still be set to auto or none; the incompatibility is specifically with forcing a named tool, not with configuring tool_choice at all.

options.text: Parallel tool-call control must be moved to the request root before a tool can be forced
options.explanation: Parallel tool-call control governs concurrent tool invocations and is unrelated to the conflict between forced tool choice and extended thinking.

options.text: Forcing a named client tool is unsupported; converting it to a server tool makes it valid
options.explanation: Changing whether a tool executes server-side or client-side does not resolve the incompatibility between forced named tool_choice and manual extended thinking.

options.text: Forced tool use conflicts with manual extended thinking; use auto or an adaptive design
options.explanation: Manual extended thinking requires the model to reason freely before acting, which a forced named-tool choice overrides, so compatibility requires auto tool choice or a design that does not force a specific tool.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A Python stdio MCP server prints progress to stdout and the host reports parse errors. What fixes it?

options.text: Wrap each progress print inside a tool result
options.explanation: Wrapping prints in tool results does not stop unrelated progress output from interleaving with JSON-RPC on stdout; the print statements themselves must move off stdout.

options.text: Log to stderr and reserve stdout for JSON-RPC
options.explanation: A stdio MCP server communicates JSON-RPC exclusively over stdout, so any print statement mixed into that stream corrupts message framing; logging must go to stderr instead.

options.text: Have the host parse stdout as one JSON array instead
options.explanation: The host expects newline-delimited individual JSON-RPC messages, not a JSON array, so reinterpreting the framing does not fix mixed plain-text and JSON-RPC content.

options.text: Switch the server to the legacy HTTP SSE transport
options.explanation: Changing transport is an unrelated and unnecessary architecture change; the actual defect is stdout being polluted with non-protocol text.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: An app needs a local stdio MCP server with resources and prompts. How should it integrate?

options.text: Pass the command as an mcp_servers URL
options.explanation: The mcp_servers connector field expects a remote HTTPS URL, not a local process launch command, so a stdio server cannot be wired in this way.

options.text: Use mcp_servers without an mcp_toolset
options.explanation: The remote connector only exposes tool calls and has no mechanism for resources or prompts regardless of toolset configuration, so it cannot satisfy this requirement.

options.text: Use its own MCP client and SDK helpers
options.explanation: A local stdio server needing resources and prompts (not just tools) requires a full MCP client implementation via SDK helpers, since the hosted Messages API connector only supports remote tool calls.

options.text: Expose it over plaintext localhost HTTP
options.explanation: The app still needs an MCP client to speak the protocol over that HTTP endpoint, and plaintext localhost adds no capability for resources or prompts by itself.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A remote server exposes read_issue and delete_issue; only read_issue may be available through the Messages API connector. Select THREE correct principles.

options.text: Define the remote server in mcp_servers and reference it from an mcp_toolset entry in tools
options.explanation: The connector is two-part: mcp_servers describes how to reach the server and an mcp_toolset entry in tools decides which of its tools are exposed; one without the other exposes nothing.

options.text: Disable by default and explicitly enable read_issue
options.explanation: Setting the toolset default to disabled and enabling only read_issue is an allowlist, so delete_issue never appears in the model's tool list at all.

options.text: Use a publicly reachable HTTPS endpoint
options.explanation: The connector talks to servers over HTTP transports only; a local stdio process or a private host it cannot reach cannot be wired in this way.

options.text: Trust destructiveHint to block delete_issue
options.explanation: destructiveHint and similar annotations are advisory metadata for hosts and models; they do not remove the tool from the list or stop a call.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A trusted user asks an agent to read an untrusted email containing malicious instructions. Where does the raw email body belong?

options.text: In the system prompt, wrapped in XML tags
options.explanation: The system prompt is the highest-authority instruction channel, so placing untrusted content there risks the model treating injected text as privileged instructions rather than as data.

options.text: As ordinary user text in the next user turn
options.explanation: Presenting the email as if it were the trusted user's own words removes the provenance signal that separates the user's real intent from injected instructions inside the email.

options.text: In an assistant message that quotes the email
options.explanation: Assistant messages represent the model's own prior output; placing external untrusted content there misrepresents its origin and can make the model treat it as something it already said.

options.text: In a tool_result block with clear provenance
options.explanation: Wrapping the untrusted email in a tool_result block, distinct from the trusted user's own instructions, lets the agent treat it as data to inspect rather than as commands to obey.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A browser agent reads untrusted pages and can change tickets. Which defense-in-depth controls help? Select THREE.

options.text: Place every fetched page in the system prompt
options.explanation: The system prompt is the highest-authority channel, so placing untrusted page content there elevates injected instructions instead of containing them.

options.text: Minimal tool scopes and approval for destructive actions
options.explanation: Narrow tool scopes bound what a hijacked agent can do, and a human approval on destructive actions means an injected instruction cannot silently change a ticket.

options.text: Screen and label tool output before model delivery
options.explanation: Screening fetched pages and labelling them as untrusted tool output before the model sees them lowers the chance that injected text is read as an instruction.

options.text: Sandbox tools and red-team with adversarial pages
options.explanation: Sandboxing limits the damage of a successful injection while adversarial testing finds injections before attackers do; each layer works even if the other fails.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A moderation pipeline needs a machine-readable decision for each comment. What design is best?

options.text: Explicit categories plus a structured JSON verdict branched on in code
options.explanation: Defined categories with a structured verdict give the pipeline a stable machine-readable signal that application code can branch on deterministically for every comment.

options.text: A prose instruction asking the model to be safe and note any concerns
options.explanation: A free-text safety instruction produces unstructured prose rather than a decision the pipeline can parse and branch on programmatically.

options.text: An assistant-turn JSON prefill so each reply starts with an opening brace
options.explanation: Prefill only nudges the shape of the reply's start; it is not a substitute for an actual defined schema and category set enforced across every classification.

options.text: Retrying the same comment until the model returns a benign-looking answer
options.explanation: Retrying until a convenient answer appears discards genuine moderation signal and produces an unreliable, non-machine-readable outcome.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: A GitHub Actions deployment needs API access without storing a long-lived secret. What is the best option?

options.text: A personal API key committed to the repository in an encrypted secrets file
options.explanation: Even encrypted at rest, this is still a long-lived static credential checked into the repository, which is exactly what the requirement rules out.

options.text: A legacy workspace key shared by every CI job and rotated manually each quarter
options.explanation: A shared static workspace key is a long-lived secret with broad blast radius across every job that uses it, not a short-lived scoped credential.

options.text: Workload Identity Federation exchanging a platform JWT for a short-lived token
options.explanation: Federation lets the CI job present its platform-issued JWT to obtain a short-lived credential on demand, so no long-lived secret ever needs to be stored in the pipeline.

options.text: An API key placed in the deployment agent's system prompt so no secret store is needed
options.explanation: Putting a credential in the system prompt both fails to eliminate the long-lived secret and exposes it to the model's context, which is worse than typical secret storage.

questions.sourceNote: Original item written to blueprint scope; not a real exam question.

questions.stem: An extraction service sees two failure kinds: some requests return HTTP 529 overloaded_error, and some return HTTP 200 whose JSON fails the app's own validation. The team retries both unchanged up to five times. Which change is correct?

options.text: Retry both classes unchanged but raise the attempt limit from five to ten, since some validation failures eventually pass on a later sample.
options.explanation: More identical attempts help only the transient class; a deterministic output defect will keep reproducing and each replay wastes tokens.

options.text: Keep retrying the 529s unchanged with backoff, but re-prompt validation failures once or twice with the specific validation error included.
options.explanation: A transport-level 529 is transient and can succeed when replayed, whereas a model-output failure tends to reproduce unchanged; feeding back the concrete error is what changes the outcome.

options.text: Stop retrying 529s because capacity errors never recover on their own, and keep retrying validation failures unchanged until one passes.
options.explanation: This inverts the two classes: overloaded_error is exactly the kind of error that backoff is for, and unchanged replays are the wrong tool for a schema miss.

options.text: Treat every failure of either class as a platform bug and open a support ticket with the request_id before allowing any retry to run.
options.explanation: Persistent 500-class errors deserve a ticket with request_id, but a 529 is a capacity signal and a validation miss is an application-side prompting problem, not a platform defect.

questions.rationale: Tests separating transport failures (retry unchanged) from model-output failures (bounded reprompt with the error).
